subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply

subjective.question: Differentiate between ciliary and flagellar movement.
subjective.answer: Ciliary and flagellar movement differ in the following ways. (1) Pattern of beat: a cilium beats with two distinct phases — a stiff effective stroke that pushes water backwards and a flexible recovery stroke that brings it back — whereas a flagellum beats in continuous undulating waves that pass along its length. (2) Coordination: cilia beat in coordinated metachronal waves over the cell surface, while a flagellum usually acts singly or in small numbers. (3) Direction of propulsion: in ciliary movement the effective stroke is at right angles to the surface and the animal moves in the direction opposite to the effective stroke; flagellar waves may push or pull the organism depending on whether the waves pass from base to tip or tip to base. (4) Examples: cilia bring about locomotion in Paramecium and larval stages, while flagella are used by Euglena, Trypanosoma and spermatozoa. (5) Both structures, however, have the same internal 9 + 2 axoneme and are powered by ATP-driven dynein arms.

subjective.question: Describe the structure of a cilium (or flagellum).
subjective.answer: A cilium or flagellum has three main parts. (1) The axoneme or shaft is the core, made of microtubules in the 9 + 2 arrangement: nine peripheral doublet microtubules surround two central single microtubules, all enclosed in a membrane continuous with the plasma membrane. The doublets carry dynein arms and are connected by nexin links; radial spokes join the doublets to the central sheath. (2) The basal body (kinetosome) lies at the base, has a 9 + 0 triplet arrangement like a centriole, and anchors the organelle. (3) Rootlets may extend into the cytoplasm for support. Bending occurs when dynein arms use ATP to slide one doublet over the next; because the doublets are linked, sliding is converted into bending.

subjective.question: Explain the effective and recovery strokes in ciliary movement. What is metachronal rhythm?
subjective.answer: In the effective (power) stroke the cilium remains stiff and extended, sweeping through the water like an oar and pushing the water backwards, so the animal is propelled forwards. In the recovery stroke the cilium bends and curls back limply to its original position, offering minimum resistance to the water. Thousands of cilia do not beat together but in a coordinated sequence called metachronal rhythm: cilia in one transverse row beat together, and successive rows beat slightly later, so waves appear to pass over the surface. This coordination makes ciliary locomotion smooth and continuous, as seen in Paramecium.

subjective.question: Write down the differences between cilia and flagella.
subjective.answer: Cilia are short (about 5–10 μm), numerous, and cover all or part of the cell surface; they beat with an effective and a recovery stroke in metachronal coordination. Flagella are long (up to 150 μm or more), few in number (usually one or two), occur at one end of the cell, and beat in undulating waves passing along their length. Both have an identical internal structure — a 9 + 2 axoneme arising from a basal body — and both are locomotory organelles that require ATP for movement.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: Describe the energy supply in muscle contraction.
subjective.answer: The immediate energy for contraction comes from ATP, which is hydrolysed by the myosin ATPase of the cross-bridges. A muscle holds only a small ATP store, enough for a few seconds, so ATP is continuously regenerated by three routes. (1) Direct phosphorylation: creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine) stored in the muscle transfers its phosphate to ADP through the enzyme creatine kinase, rapidly rebuilding ATP; this supports about 10–15 seconds of activity. (2) Anaerobic glycolysis: glucose or glycogen is broken down to pyruvic acid and, in the absence of enough oxygen, to lactic acid, giving a small net gain of 2 ATP per glucose; this is fast but produces lactic acid and fatigue. (3) Aerobic respiration (oxidative phosphorylation): in the mitochondria, pyruvic acid and fatty acids are completely oxidized to CO2 and water, yielding a large amount of ATP (about 30 or more per glucose); this is slower but is the main source for prolonged, moderate activity.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: Explain the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
subjective.answer: According to the sliding filament theory (Huxley and Hanson), contraction occurs when the thin actin filaments slide inward between the thick myosin filaments, pulling the Z lines closer together; the filaments themselves do not shorten. When Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, it binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads (cross-bridges) then attach to actin, and using energy from ATP they bend (power stroke), dragging the actin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. ATP then binds to the myosin head, detaching it, and the cycle repeats. As a result the I band and H zone shorten while the A band stays the same length, and the whole muscle contracts.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: What is a sarcomere? Describe its bands and zones.
subjective.answer: A sarcomere is the part of a myofibril between two successive Z lines; it is the smallest contractile unit of the muscle. It contains: the A band, the dark central band of thick myosin filaments (with overlapping actin at its edges); the I band, the light band of thin actin filaments only, bisected by the Z line; and the H zone, the lighter central part of the A band where only myosin filaments are present, sometimes with an M line in its middle. During contraction the sarcomere shortens because the I band and H zone narrow, while the A band remains constant.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: What is oxygen debt? How is lactic acid removed from the body after exercise?
subjective.answer: After vigorous exercise the body needs extra oxygen over and above the resting requirement; this additional oxygen is the oxygen debt. During exercise, ATP was partly supplied anaerobically, so lactic acid accumulated and creatine phosphate and ATP stores were depleted. In the recovery period the extra oxygen is used to: (1) oxidize part of the lactic acid to CO2 and water in the liver and muscles, (2) reconvert the remaining lactic acid to glycogen (Cori cycle in the liver), (3) rebuild ATP and creatine phosphate stores, and (4) reload myoglobin with oxygen. Heavy breathing after exercise continues until this debt is repaid.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: Explain the roles of Ca2+ and ATP in muscle contraction. What is rigor mortis?
subjective.answer: Ca2+ acts as the switch of contraction: released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum on stimulation, it binds to troponin and exposes the active sites on actin so that cross-bridges can form; when Ca2+ is pumped back, the muscle relaxes. ATP has three roles: it provides energy for the power stroke of the myosin head, it detaches the myosin head from actin at the end of each cycle, and it powers the Ca2+ pump of the sarcoplasmic reticulum during relaxation. If ATP is absent after death, the cross-bridges cannot detach and the muscles become stiff — this is rigor mortis, which passes off later as the proteins break down.

subjective.topic: Muscle Contraction and Its Energy Supply
subjective.question: What is muscle fatigue? Write its causes.
subjective.answer: Muscle fatigue is the decline in the ability of a muscle to contract after prolonged activity. Its main causes are: (1) accumulation of lactic acid, which lowers the pH and interferes with enzyme activity and cross-bridge function; (2) depletion of ATP, creatine phosphate and glycogen stores; (3) accumulation of ADP and inorganic phosphate; and (4) shortage of oxygen during continued anaerobic work. Rest allows the lactic acid to be removed, stores to be rebuilt and the oxygen debt to be repaid, so the muscle recovers.

subjective.question: Explain the resting membrane potential of a neuron and how it is maintained.
subjective.answer: The resting membrane potential is the electrical potential difference (about –70 mV) across the membrane of an unstimulated neuron, the inside being negative relative to the outside. It is produced and maintained because: (1) the membrane is much more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so K+ leaks out, leaving unbalanced negative ions (proteins and phosphates) inside; (2) the sodium-potassium pump (Na+/K+ ATPase) actively transports 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in for each ATP hydrolysed, keeping the Na+ concentration high outside and K+ high inside. Together these keep the resting neuron polarized and ready to fire an impulse.

subjective.question: Describe the events of an action potential.
subjective.answer: An action potential is a brief reversal of the membrane potential that travels along the axon as the nerve impulse. When a stimulus of threshold strength is applied, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in; the membrane depolarizes from –70 mV to about +30 mV. Immediately afterwards the Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open; K+ flows out and the membrane is repolarized back to the resting value. A brief hyperpolarization may follow before the resting potential is restored. The action potential is self-propagating and follows the all-or-none law: it either fires at full amplitude or not at all.

subjective.question: What is saltatory conduction? Why is it faster than continuous conduction?
subjective.answer: Saltatory conduction is the jumping of a nerve impulse from one node of Ranvier to the next in a myelinated fibre. The myelin sheath insulates the axon, so the action potential can only be regenerated at the exposed nodes, where the ion channels are concentrated; the electrical current spreads rapidly through the insulated internode. This makes conduction much faster (up to about 120 m/s) than in unmyelinated fibres, and it also saves energy because ion pumping is needed only at the nodes.

subjective.question: Describe the transmission of a nerve impulse across a synapse.
subjective.answer: When a nerve impulse reaches the synaptic knob of the presynaptic neuron, the depolarization opens Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ enters the knob. This causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release a neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis. The transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and producing a new potential (excitatory or inhibitory) in the postsynaptic cell. The transmitter is then quickly removed — acetylcholine is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase — so that the synapse is ready for the next impulse. Synapses ensure one-way transmission of impulses.

subjective.question: What is meant by transduction of impulse (sensory transduction)? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy (light, sound, pressure, chemicals) into electrical signals (receptor potentials and then nerve impulses) by sensory receptor cells. Each receptor is specific for one kind of stimulus: photoreceptors of the retina convert light into impulses, hair cells of the organ of Corti convert sound vibrations into impulses, olfactory receptors convert chemical stimuli into impulses, and mechanoreceptors of the skin convert pressure and touch into impulses. If the receptor potential reaches threshold, action potentials are generated in the sensory neuron and carried to the central nervous system, where the sensation is perceived.

subjective.question: Write a short note on cranial nerves.
subjective.answer: The cranial nerves are the twelve pairs of nerves that arise directly from the brain (mainly the brain stem) and supply the head, neck and most internal organs. They are numbered I–XII from front to back: I Olfactory (smell), II Optic (vision), III Oculomotor (eye movement), IV Trochlear (eye movement), V Trigeminal (sensations from face, chewing), VI Abducens (eye movement), VII Facial (facial expression, taste), VIII Vestibulocochlear (hearing and balance), IX Glossopharyngeal (taste, swallowing), X Vagus (organs of chest and abdomen), XI Accessory (neck muscles) and XII Hypoglossal (tongue movements). Some are purely sensory (I, II, VIII), some purely motor (III, IV, VI, XI, XII) and some mixed (V, VII, IX, X).

subjective.question: Classify the cranial nerves into sensory, motor and mixed nerves, giving examples of each.
subjective.answer: Sensory cranial nerves carry impulses from sense organs to the brain only: I Olfactory (smell), II Optic (vision) and VIII Vestibulocochlear (hearing and equilibrium). Motor cranial nerves carry impulses from the brain to muscles only: III Oculomotor, IV Trochlear and VI Abducens (movements of the eyeball), XI Accessory (sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles) and XII Hypoglossal (tongue muscles). Mixed cranial nerves contain both sensory and motor fibres: V Trigeminal (facial sensation and chewing muscles), VII Facial (taste and facial expression), IX Glossopharyngeal (taste, swallowing) and X Vagus (sensation and movement in the pharynx, larynx and viscera).

subjective.question: Describe the structure of the mammalian ear.
subjective.answer: The mammalian ear has three parts. (1) The external ear consists of the pinna, which collects sound waves, and the auditory canal, which conducts them to the tympanic membrane (eardrum). (2) The middle ear is an air-filled cavity containing three small bones, the ear ossicles — malleus, incus and stapes — which transmit and amplify the vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window; it is connected to the pharynx by the Eustachian tube, which equalizes air pressure on the two sides of the eardrum. (3) The inner ear, enclosed in the skull bone, contains the cochlea (the organ of hearing, bearing the organ of Corti), and the vestibule and semicircular canals concerned with balance.

subjective.question: Write a note on hearing in vertebrates.
subjective.answer: Hearing means the detection of sound vibrations by specialized receptors and their conversion into nerve impulses. In terrestrial vertebrates, sound waves are collected by the external ear and strike the tympanic membrane, which vibrates. In mammals the vibrations are transmitted and amplified by the three ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) to the oval window; in birds, reptiles and amphibians a single bone, the columella, does this work. Vibrations of the oval window set up pressure waves in the fluid (perilymph and endolymph) of the cochlea. These waves make the basilar membrane vibrate, bending the hair cells of the organ of Corti against the tectorial membrane. Bending of the hair cells is transduced into nerve impulses, which travel through the vestibulocochlear (auditory) nerve to the brain, where sound is perceived. Fishes, which lack an external ear, detect vibrations in water mainly through the inner ear and the lateral line system.

subjective.question: Explain how sound is transduced into nerve impulses in the cochlea.
subjective.answer: Sound transduction takes place in the organ of Corti of the cochlea. Pressure waves in the cochlear fluid, set up by the stapes at the oval window, travel through the scala vestibuli and scala tympani and cause a region of the basilar membrane to vibrate (high-pitched sounds near the base, low-pitched sounds near the apex). The sensory hair cells of the organ of Corti sit on the basilar membrane with their hairs touching the stiff tectorial membrane above. When the basilar membrane moves, the hairs are bent; this opens ion channels in the hair cells, producing a receptor potential and releasing neurotransmitter onto the fibres of the auditory nerve. The resulting impulses reach the auditory area of the brain, giving the sensation of hearing.

subjective.question: Write a note on olfaction in mammals. Why is the sense of smell so acute in a dog?
subjective.answer: Olfaction is the sense of smell, in which airborne chemicals are detected by olfactory receptor neurons in the olfactory epithelium lining the upper part of the nasal cavity. These receptors are chemoreceptors; their impulses pass through the olfactory nerve (I) to the olfactory bulbs of the brain. A dog's sense of smell is exceptionally acute because it has about 300 million olfactory receptors compared with only about 5 million in man, a much larger olfactory epithelium, and a proportionally larger part of the brain devoted to analysing smells. This is why dogs can track scents, detect buried objects and identify individuals by smell.

subjective.question: Describe the roles of the myelin sheath and the nodes of Ranvier in nerve conduction.
subjective.answer: The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer formed by Schwann cells around the axons of many neurons. It greatly increases the speed of conduction because the impulse jumps between the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), and it also protects the axon and reduces energy loss. Nodes of Ranvier are the short gaps between adjacent Schwann cells where the axon membrane is exposed; they are crowded with voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels, and the action potential is regenerated only at these nodes. Loss of myelin (demyelination) slows or blocks impulse conduction.
